articles.title: US-Canada trade war escalates amid tit-for-tat tariffs
articles.author: Prashant Rao
articles.summary: The US-Canada trade war intensified, with Washington moving to ban a raft of goods from its northern neighbour after Ottawa imposed retaliatory tariffs on its biggest trading partner. The moves follow escalating rhetoric between the pair’s leaders, though a senior Trump administration official said the countries would try to negotiate an offramp from the dispute . Any truce or deal looks unlikely to permanently repair what was once a close alliance, however: The row is derailing any hope of renewing the USMCA North American trade pact, and Canada is increasingly looking to shift away from its dependence on the US. “When the old path disappears,” one analyst wrote in The Globe and Mail, “ the only option is to change direction .” — Prashant Rao

articles.title: Record gas prices squeeze Americans as summer travel season ends, midterms loom and Iran war wages on
articles.summary: As the summer travel season came to a close, Americans faced the most expensive Labor Day at the pump on record, extending the squeeze on household budgets for millions who hit the road over the holiday weekend. AAA estimated that nearly 40 million Americans would drive over the holiday, paying unprecedented prices for gasoline. The national average for regular gasoline reached $4.15 per gallon on Tuesday, up about 5 cents from the previous week and nearly 96 cents higher than a year earlier. The price shattered the previous Labor Day record of $3.82, set in 2012, and marked the first time the national average topped $4 during the holiday weekend. FORGET GASOLINE: THIS OVERLOOKED FUEL COULD RAISE THE PRICE OF NEARLY EVERYTHING YOU BUY The spike came despite a seasonal trend that typically brings some relief after Labor Day, when summer travel winds down and gasoline demand eases. This year, however, elevated crude oil prices tied to the Iran conflict offset that typical decline. Fighting in the Middle East raised concerns about disruptions to oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz , a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that carries roughly one-fifth of the world's crude oil.

The heart of Manhattan was a decadent playground for the wealthy, while outlying neighborhoods were plagued by desperate poverty and violence. I grew up only 200 miles away, and yet my parents never took me there as a kid. But if New York felt menacing and foreign to them, in reality, it is the most American of cities. articles.summary: Firefighters look through debris from the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001. Photo by Peter Turnley/Getty Images Friday marks 25 years since September 11, 2001. Twenty-five years. Hard to believe. For my generation, 9/11 was our “Where were you when JFK was assassinated?” moment. Almost everyone who lived through that day remembers where they were, who they were with, and how they first heard that something unimaginable was happening in New York. I was in London, a young Muslim researcher at a British television company, sitting on the ninth floor of a skyscraper. I’d started the job only days earlier. It was early afternoon for us when the images came on the TV. My new colleagues and I had just returned to our desks from lunch. And… wait… hold on… a plane had flown into the World Trade Center? We all stared at the screen, stunned and confused, trying to work out what the hell was happening. Was it a freak accident? Or an… attack ? I vividly remember this random guy walking past our desks, looking up at the TV on the wall, and saying: “What have the Palestinians done now?” Think about that. We didn’t know what had happened. We didn’t know who was responsible. But already: Arabs.

articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu threatened to sue Haaretz over its report that he ignored the UAE president’s explicit warning about Hamas’ Oct. 7 attacks, revelations that caused uproar in Israel and widened Netanyahu’s rift with Abu Dhabi. The allegations, which Netanyahu denies, have energized his domestic opponents, some of whom are viewed more favorably in Abu Dhabi, ahead of critical Israeli elections next month; polls show the prime minister appears to be losing ground. Netanyahu is targeting a record seventh term but faces hawkish candidates who blame him for undermining national security . “Everyone in Israel shares a sense of historical crisis, and his name is all over it ,” an Israeli analyst told Reuters. — Brendan Ruberry

stories.summary: US long-term bond yields spiked to three-year highs Wednesday after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s bond buybacks failed to impress markets. Borrowing costs leapt higher in part because investors expected more firepower, a Deutsche Bank strategist told Bloomberg: “It’s like Treasury created this monster that it now has to keep feeding.” Bessent’s smaller-than-expected move suggests he’s accepted a “limited role” for buybacks, Evercore ISI analysts wrote, which aren’t likely to reverse yields without addressing the “direction of the debt and deficit,” a Société Générale researcher said. “ Everything else is cosmetic .” Bessent is juggling multiple interventions, daring traders to take the opposite side of his yen purchases. “I have asymmetric information. I am the house now ,” he said Tuesday. — Brendan Ruberry

stories.summary: Houthi rebels on Wednesday said Saudi Arabia launched airstrikes in Yemen, as hostilities between Riyadh and the Iran-backed militia escalate toward all-out war. Saudi had vowed to retaliate after the Houthis carried out their largest attack on the kingdom since a 2022 ceasefire , injuring 73 people and disrupting oil production. Riyadh is now contending with simultaneous disruptions to both of its primary shipping lanes, in the Red Sea’s Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Strait of Hormuz, as the kingdom’s oil exports fell to 13-year lows. The Houthis see the current conflict as a “ golden opportunity ” to change the balance of power, a Middle East expert told The New York Times. “A reduction in hostilities any time soon seems unlikely,” ACLED wrote. — Brendan Ruberry

articles.title: Smithsonian chief to retire after clashes with White House
articles.author: Rebecca Falconer
articles.summary: Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch announced he will retire later this year following clashes with the White House. Why it matters: Bunch's departure leaves the Smithsonian facing a leadership transition as the Trump administration escalates efforts to reshape how the institution presents American history. Driving the news: Bunch will step down by the end of the year after nearly 38 years at the Smithsonian, the institution said Tuesday. "It is time for my next chapter, a chapter that will allow me to continue to protect the integrity of the Smithsonian and to champion the importance of a history that illuminates and celebrates the complex story of our nation," the 73-year-old said. Flashback: Bunch pushed back against a White House review of the Smithsonian in a July message to staff, saying the report was "not a fair characterization" of the National Museum of American History. He said the Smithsonian remained committed to "scholarship, nonpartisanship, independence, accuracy, and integrity."
